claim: LLMs answering multiple-choice questions have a systematic preference for particular option IDs (e.g. 'A' or 'C') that is largely a prior over the ID tokens rather than option position, so moving all gold answers to one letter swings MMLU accuracy by up to ~15-18 points (e.g. llama-30B 53.1 -> 68.2 when gold is always A), and removing IDs (not shuffling them) removes most of the bias; debiasing instructions and CoT do not fix it.

paper.title: Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors
paper.citation_source: Semantic Scholar Graph API batch POST https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/batch?fields=title,citationCount,publicationDate,venue with id arXiv:2309.03882 (paperclip index shows 228)
paper.s2_batch_record_title: Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors

experiment.location_in_paper: Section 1 Table 1 (answer-moving attack), Section 2.2-2.6 (RStd metric, ablations; Table 2), Section 3-4 (PriDe; Fig 4-5), Appendix B/C (all 20 models)
experiment.task_or_benchmark: MMLU (4-option, 57 subjects), ARC-Challenge (4-option), CommonsenseQA (5-option); 2/3-option variants constructed
experiment.intervention_or_prompts:
Standard prompt 'Question: ...
Options:
A. ..
B. ..
Answer:'; answer-moving attack (move gold to A/B/C/D); shuffle option IDs; remove option IDs (cloze scoring); alternative ID symbols (a/b/c/d, 1/2/3/4, (A)); explicit debiasing system instruction; zero-shot CoT ('Let's think step by step'); 0-shot and 5-shot.
experiment.evaluation_procedure: Open models: argmax over output probabilities of option ID tokens; gpt-3.5-turbo: first generated token at temperature 0 (100 samples to approximate probabilities for PriDe). Selection bias measured by std of per-ID recalls (RStd).
experiment.metric: Accuracy; RStd (standard deviation of recall across option IDs); chi-square test on prediction proportions.
experiment.main_comparison: Accuracy when gold moved to each position vs original; RStd under default vs shuffled IDs vs removed IDs vs prompting strategies; PriDe vs cyclic/full permutation debiasing.
experiment.main_result: 0-shot MMLU (Table 1): llama-30B 53.1 orig, 68.2 when gold always A, 41.2 when always D; falcon-inst-40B 51.5 -> 69.1 (D) / 38.3 (A); gpt-3.5-turbo 67.2 -> 74.2 (C) / 60.9 (D). On a label-balanced 1,000-question MMLU sample llama-30B picks A/B/C/D 34.6/27.3/22.3/15.8%. gpt-3.5-turbo MMLU RStd: default 5.5, shuffling IDs 5.1, removing IDs 1.0, debiasing instruction 6.1, CoT 4.5. PriDe with 5% estimation samples reduces RStd and raises accuracy at low cost.

downstream.title: When Benchmarks are Targets: Revealing the Sensitivity of Large Language Model Leaderboards
downstream.summary: Confirms selection bias in all tested LLMs (0/5-shot) and that shuffling answer order changes leaderboard rankings, but argues Zheng et al.'s shuffle-IDs evidence that position bias is minor is inconclusive; with rare symbols, token and position bias are hard to disentangle (read Sec 5.2).

downstream.title: Look at the Text: Instruction-Tuned Language Models are More Robust Multiple Choice Selectors than You Think
downstream.summary: For instruction-tuned models, first-token probabilities often mismatch the generated text answer; text answers show small selection bias and, when mismatch >50%, less bias than PriDe-debiased first-token probabilities. Suggests part of the measured bias is an artifact of logit-based scoring (read abstract, Sec 1).

downstream.title: Changing Answer Order Can Decrease MMLU Accuracy
downstream.summary: Shuffling MMLU answer contents (labels fixed) lowers all 10 open models' test-retest accuracy; Llama-3-70B-Instruct drops least (80.3 -> 75.3 'both-correct' metric), Falcon-40B-Instruct and Gemma-7B-it most (~27%). Note the metric requires correctness on original and shuffled versions (read Sec 2-3, Table 1).

downstream.title: Unveiling Selection Biases: Exploring Order and Token Sensitivity in Large Language Models
downstream.summary: Quantifies both option-order and token sensitivity across several models and tasks in zero-shot and proposes mitigations (abstract/intro read).

downstream.title: Mitigating Selection Bias in Large Language Models via Permutation-Aware GRPO
downstream.summary: Treats selection bias (position + label-symbol) as still present in current LLMs for MCQ and LLM-as-judge and proposes RL training to enforce permutation consistency (abstract/intro only).

downstream_summary: Selection bias under symbol (first-token) scoring is widely replicated, including on Llama-3-era open models. Two qualifications follow. How much comes from token bias versus position bias is contested (Alzahrani et al. 2024). The size of the bias depends on scoring method: generated text answers from instruction-tuned models are much less biased (Wang et al. 2024). The effect is smaller for stronger models. I found no systematic re-test on 2025-26 frontier or reasoning models.
notability_notes: ICLR 2024 spotlight, 20 models, released code + outputs; standard reference for MCQ selection bias and PriDe debiasing; motivates answer-shuffling in benchmark practice.
gaps: The per-model breakdown for all 20 models (Appendix B) was not transcribed. No frontier-model (GPT-4o/Claude/Gemini 2.x, reasoning models) replication read.
